data.generator_code:
def generate(rng, n):
    size = max(1, min(n, 20))
    matrix = [[rng.randint(-1000, 1000) for _ in range(size)] for _ in range(size)]
    return [matrix]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    size = max(1, min(n, 20))
    matrix = [[rng.randint(-1000, 1000) for _ in range(size)] for _ in range(size)]
    return [matrix]

data.key_insight: Rotating a matrix 90 degrees clockwise is equivalent to first transposing the matrix (swapping elements across the main diagonal) and then reversing each of its rows.

steps.title: Transpose the Matrix
steps.detail: Iterate through the matrix for row i from 0 to n-1 and column j from i+1 to n-1, swapping matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i].

steps.title: Reverse each row
steps.detail: Iterate through each row of the transposed matrix and reverse its elements in-place using a two-pointer approach or slicing.

data.pattern_summary: Manipulating 2D grid coordinates systematically, often using geometric operations like transposing and reversing to achieve rotations without extra space.

pattern_options.name: Matrix transformation
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We map old coordinates (r, c) to new coordinates (c, n - 1 - r) to perform the rotation.

pattern_options.name: Depth-first search
pattern_options.feedback: DFS explores graphs or trees by traversing paths deeply, which does not apply to geometric grid rotation.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Sliding window optimizes subarray or substring problems on 1D sequences, not 2D matrix rotations.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Two pointers shrink or expand search spaces from ends inward, which fails to handle 2D rotational coordinate mapping.

signals.hint: Indicates a specific geometric coordinate mapping is required.
Restricts us from allocating a second full 2D matrix for the output.

data.brute_force_idea: Create a complete copy of the matrix first, then iterate through every cell and place it into its new rotated position in the original matrix.
data.brute_force_why: We must visit every single element in the n x n matrix to read it and write it.
data.bottleneck: The direct approach uses O(n^2) time and O(n^2) space to copy the matrix. Since every element must be moved, O(n^2) time is theoretically minimal.
bottleneck_hints: Count how many elements exist in an n x n matrix.
Consider if you can avoid visiting every element at least once.
Recognize that touching every element once sets a lower bound of O(n^2) time complexity.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach wastes space by copying the entire matrix to remember original positions. The optimized solution removes this bottleneck by performing two in-place geometric operations: first transposing the matrix across its main diagonal, then reversing each row.

derivation.note: Iterates through the upper triangle, running about n(n-1)/2 total times.
Swaps elements across the diagonal, scaling with line 7.
Iterates through each row for reversal.

data.time_summary: Lines 7 and 8 dominate the execution, running proportional to n squared as confirmed by the step counts scaling from 10 steps at n=4 to 210 steps at n=32. Thus, the total time complexity is O(n^2).
data.space_summary: The algorithm modifies the matrix in-place using a constant number of variables for indexing and swapping, resulting in O(1) auxiliary space.
data.takeaway: When rotating a 2D grid in-place, break the rotation down into simpler symmetric matrix transformations like transposition and reflection.
mistakes: Starting the inner loop at j = 0 instead of j = i + 1 during the transpose, which would swap elements back to their original positions.
Forgetting that matrix.reverse() operates in-place and trying to assign its return value, which evaluates to None.
Allocating a secondary data structure when an in-place modification is required.

events.label: Tutor: build the visual explanation

data.overview: The Rotate Image algorithm rotates an n x n 2D matrix 90 degrees clockwise in-place. It achieves this by first transposing the matrix (swapping elements across the main diagonal) and then reversing each individual row.
data.intuition: Imagine holding a square paper and flipping its corners over the diagonal crease, then folding or flipping the entire page horizontally left-to-right. The final result is a perfect 90-degree clockwise rotation.
